rows.grounds: sat (being, existent) + iti (thus), stating the condition of existence
asat (non-existent) + kāryatā (effect-ness) + āśaṅkā (doubt), doubt that an effect arises from non-existence

items.question: How can doubt about effects arising from non-existence persist if reality is eternally existent?
premises: Reality is eternally existent.
Doubt concerns effects arising from non-existence.
Eternal existence challenges the basis of such doubt.
items.inference: If being is eternal, the suspicion that effects come from non-existence is untenable.
items.plain_english: If being is eternal indeed, how can there be doubt that an effect arises from non-existence?

rows.grounds: instrumental of something distinct or separate
kartr (agent) + ādi (and others), causal factors such as agent
syuḥ (may be) + te (they), hypothetical existence of those factors
tat (that) + ātmaka (nature), having a nature distinct from the effect

items.question: Can causal factors produce an effect if they are entirely separate in nature from it?
premises: Agents and other causal factors may be posited.
These factors may be separate from the effect.
Separation raises doubt about their capacity to constitute the effect.
items.inference: If causal factors are wholly separate in nature, their role in producing the effect is problematic.
items.plain_english: If agents and other factors are separate and of a nature distinct from it, can they be so?

rows.grounds: vyatiriktaiḥ (by separate things) + tu (but), contrasting with the previous case
sadbhiḥ (by existing things) + api (even), granting their existence
source or basis taken as non-existent
the state or fact of being born or arising

items.question: How could birth arise from non-existence even through separate existing causal factors?
premises: Causal factors may be separate and existing.
The effect is considered as arising from non-existence.
Existing separate factors do not bridge non-existence to existence.
items.inference: Even existing separate causes cannot explain the birth of something from non-existence.
items.plain_english: But even by separate existing things, how could birth arise from what is non-existent?

rows.grounds: janma (birth) + kāla (time), the moment of origination
ghaṭa (pot) + abhāva (absence), absence of the pot at that time
relation or contact between effect and causes
causal instruments or factors involved in production

items.question: Can a non-existent effect have any connection with causal instruments at the moment of birth?
premises: At the time of birth the pot is absent.
Connection requires relata to be present.
Absent entities cannot relate to causal instruments.
items.inference: There can be no connection between causal instruments and an absent effect at birth.
items.plain_english: At the time of birth, because of the absence of the pot, there is indeed no connection with the causal instruments.

rows.grounds: vyañjaka (manifestor) + api (also), the factor that would reveal it

items.question: Why would an effect remain unperceived even if it were somehow considered existent?
premises: An effect might be claimed to exist.
Perception requires a manifesting condition.
Absence of a manifestor prevents perception.
items.inference: Even if existent, the effect would be unperceived due to the absence of a manifestor.
items.plain_english: Even if it exists, that effect would be unperceived because of the absence of a manifestor.

rows.grounds: sat (existent) + kārya (effect) + vāda (doctrine), the view that the effect pre-exists in the cause

items.question: What doctrine resolves the problems raised against effects arising from non-existence?
premises: Prior objections target origination from non-existence.
A doctrine affirming pre-existent effects addresses these objections.
The doctrine is named satkāryavāda.
items.inference: The doctrine of the pre-existent effect is the proposed resolution.
items.plain_english: This is the doctrine of the pre-existent effect.

rows.grounds: itaḥ (from this) + api (also), introducing another reason

items.question: In what way is the pot different from the lump of clay as its material cause?
premises: The effect should be understood as pre-existent.
The pot arises from a lump of clay.
If not different in substance, the effect is not newly created.
items.inference: The pot is not substantially different from the clay, supporting the pre-existent effect view.
items.plain_english: Know from this also that the effect is pre-existent: in what way is the pot different from the lump of clay?

rows.grounds: anupādānatā (state of not being material cause) + eva (indeed), consequence of non-difference
demonstrative referring to the cause or substance

items.question: What follows if the pot and clay are held to be completely non-different in nature?
premises: Non-difference between cause and effect is considered.
If non-different, the clay would cease to be a material cause.
Identity would mean the effect is simply the cause.
items.inference: Complete non-difference implies the clay is not a material cause and the pot is just that clay.
items.plain_english: If there is non-difference, it would indeed not be a material cause; that would be just it.

items.question: Why does the doctrine of the pre-existent effect entail the indestructibility of the effect?
premises: The pre-existent effect is already established.
What is truly established does not newly perish.
Indestructibility follows from pre-existence.
items.inference: Because the effect is pre-existent and established, it is indestructible.
items.plain_english: For the pre-existent effect is indeed established; therefore there is indestructibility.

rows.grounds: hema (gold) + vat (like), analogy for persistent substance
sarva (all) + loka (world) + anusāra (accordance), following common experience
in the same manner as previously stated

items.question: What common illustration supports the persistence of substance through changing forms?
premises: The argument follows common worldly understanding.
Gold persists through different ornaments.
This analogy illustrates the pre-existent effect.
items.inference: The example of gold, as before, illustrates persistence through transformation.
items.plain_english: Thus, in accordance with common experience, the illustration is given as before: like gold.

rows.grounds: apparent loss of a particular form

items.question: How can destruction and existence be attributed simultaneously to the same underlying substance?
premises: A form such as a bracelet may cease.
Another form such as an earring may come to be.
The underlying substance persists through both.
items.inference: Destruction applies to form while existence applies to the underlying substance.
items.plain_english: There is destruction in the form of a bracelet and existence in the form of an earring and so on.

rows.grounds: saṃsthāna (configuration, arrangement) + api (also), even in form or structure

items.question: What must be examined about the nature of difference within configurations of the same substance?
premises: Configurations appear to differ.
Difference in configuration requires analysis.
The analysis bears on the status of substance and form.
items.inference: Difference even in configuration must be carefully considered.
items.plain_english: Even in configuration, difference should be considered.

rows.grounds: śiva (Śiva) + tva (ness), the nature or reality of Śiva
a (not) + vyāpta (pervaded), not encompassed by Śiva-ness
vā (or) + abhidhīyatām (should be stated), demanding a clear position

items.question: Should configurations be declared as pervaded by Śiva-ness or as not pervaded by it?
premises: Configurations are under examination.
They may be pervaded by Śiva-ness or not.
A definite position must be stated.
items.inference: The status of configurations relative to Śiva-ness must be explicitly determined.
items.plain_english: Should it be stated that it is pervaded by Śiva-ness, or not pervaded?

rows.grounds: in either of the two alternatives
a defect or problem in the position

items.question: What problem arises if configurations are described as either pervaded or not pervaded by Śiva-ness?
premises: Two alternatives were proposed regarding pervasion by Śiva-ness.
Each alternative can be stated.
Stating either alternative leads to difficulty.
items.inference: Both alternatives entail a fault.
items.plain_english: If stated in either way, there is a fault.

rows.grounds: na (not) + evam (thus), rejecting the alleged fault
in the case of their destruction
in our view or for us
na (not) + iṣṭatā (desired state), not accepted as real destruction

items.question: Why is the alleged fault rejected regarding the destruction of beings in this doctrine?
premises: A fault was claimed for both alternatives.
The doctrine does not accept real destruction of beings.
Rejection of real destruction removes the fault.
items.inference: The fault does not arise because real destruction of beings is not accepted.
items.plain_english: Not so, because in the destruction of beings, real destruction is not accepted by us.

rows.grounds: nāśa (destruction) + tva (ness), the mere fact of being called destruction

items.question: What reason is given for not accepting destruction as ultimately real?
premises: Destruction is spoken of as a condition.
Being called destruction does not establish absolute non-existence.
The doctrine treats such destruction as non-ultimate.
items.inference: Mere designation as destruction does not make it ultimately real.
items.plain_english: Because it is merely called destruction.

rows.grounds: would follow as an unwanted consequence

items.question: What undesirable consequence follows if manifestation itself is taken to be destructible?
premises: Manifestation might be considered destructible.
Destruction of manifestation would require further account.
This leads to an endless regress.
items.inference: If manifestation were destructible, endlessness would result.
items.plain_english: Even if manifestation were destructible, endlessness would result.

rows.grounds: an (non) + abhivyakti (manifestation), state of being unmanifest
continued to exist in that state

items.question: How is apparent disappearance explained without admitting absolute non-existence of the entity?
premises: Manifestation may cease.
Cessation of manifestation is non-manifestation.
The entity remains hidden rather than destroyed.
items.inference: What appears as disappearance is the same entity remaining hidden in non-manifestation.
items.plain_english: That indeed is non-manifestation; it remained hidden then.

rows.grounds: ghaṭa (pot) + ādi (etc.), particular objects as examples
in the nature or reality of Śiva

items.question: In what mode do objects like pots persist when they are not manifestly present?
premises: Objects such as pots appear and disappear.
Disappearance is explained as concealment.
Their persistence is grounded in Śiva-ness.
items.inference: Objects like pots remain hidden in the mode of Śiva-ness when unmanifest.
items.plain_english: Thus, the pot and so on remained hidden then in the nature of Śiva.

rows.grounds: abhāva (non-existence) + prāpta (attained) + rūpa (form), something that has become non-existent

items.question: Why is it impossible to produce again something that has truly attained non-existence?
premises: Production requires a basis for re-emergence.
Absolute non-existence provides no such basis.
Therefore renewed making is not fitting.
items.inference: What has truly become non-existent cannot be produced again.
items.plain_english: It is not fitting to produce again something that has attained the form of non-existence.

rows.grounds: utpatti (origination) + vināśa (destruction) + anyathā (otherwise) + anupapatti (impossibility), impossibility of explaining them otherwise
sarva (all) + śivatā (Śiva-ness), the state of everything being Śiva

items.question: How does the impossibility of explaining origination and destruction otherwise establish universal Śiva-ness?
premises: Origination and destruction cannot be explained otherwise.
The alternative explanations lead to contradictions.
Universal Śiva-ness resolves these contradictions.
items.inference: Because origination and destruction cannot be otherwise explained, the Śiva-ness of all is established.
items.plain_english: Thus, because origination and destruction cannot be explained otherwise, the Śiva-ness of all is established.

rows.grounds: itaḥ (from this) + ca (and/also), introducing another reason
the state of everything being Śiva

items.question: Why cannot universal Śiva-ness be derived from the mere aggregation of parts?
premises: Universal Śiva-ness is being established.
Parts are distinct components.
Unity of all cannot arise from parts alone.
items.inference: Universal Śiva-ness does not come from parts anywhere.
items.plain_english: And from this also, the Śiva-ness of all does not come from parts anywhere.

rows.grounds: in things that are divided or distinct

items.question: How are unity and non-difference understood to be established among divided things?
premises: Things appear divided.
Unity and non-difference are nonetheless affirmed.
Their establishment must be explained in that context.
items.inference: Unity and non-difference are established among the divided as determined in that context.
items.plain_english: As unity and non-difference are established there among the divided.

rows.grounds: in what is undivided or non-different
the state of being divided or distinct
bhinneṣu (in divided things) + api (also), even among the divided
the state of being undivided or identical

items.question: By what principle can difference appear in the undivided while non-difference remains in the divided?
premises: The undivided is the underlying reality.
Difference appears within it.
Non-difference persists even among divided appearances.
items.inference: The same principle that allows difference in the undivided also grounds non-difference among the divided.
items.plain_english: By which there is difference in the undivided, there is also non-difference even among the divided.
